method.title: Show the math
method.intro: Every number in this tool, where it comes from, and how we got it.

acreFoot.def: The water it takes to cover one acre one foot deep, about 326,000 gallons.

et.def: Water that leaves a field as vapor, from the soil and through the crop's leaves.

et0.def: How much water a standard grass field would use in this weather, the starting point for crop water needs.

worst1in5.def: Your average profit in the 4 worst years out of the last 20.

frontier.def: The set of plans where you cannot get more average profit without doing worse in bad years.

soilScore.def: A 0 to 100 score for how much a rotation builds soil: legumes, living roots, residue, low tillage, and variety.

shadowPrice.def: What one more acre-foot is worth to you, in extra profit per acre.

grace.def: NASA twin satellites that weigh changes in water stored underground by measuring tiny shifts in Earth's gravity.

power.def: NASA's daily weather records for any spot on Earth, built from satellites and weather models.

fallow.def: Land left unplanted and unwatered for a season or a year.

rotation.def: The order of crops you grow on the same field over the seasons.

plan.maxShare: Most you would plant of each rotation
plan.waterCostHelp: Leave at $0 if your crop budgets already count water.
plan.efficiencyHelp: Drip and good scheduling raise this. Higher means less water per acre for the same crop.
plan.mixTitle: Based on 20 past years, this mix fits {{water}} AF per acre in every year
plan.worstHelp: Average of the 4 worst years out of 20.
plan.overBudget: Your current plan needs {{need}} AF per acre in its highest year. Your budget is {{budget}}. It does not fit.
plan.waterValueTitle: One more acre-foot is worth {{v}} per acre to you
plan.waterValueBody: If you could get 0.1 more acre-feet per acre, your plan would earn about {{tenth}} more per acre. Use this when you price leased or banked water.
plan.waterValueZero: Water is not your limit right now
plan.waterValueZeroBody: Your soil minimum or your risk setting decides this plan. Extra water would not change it.
plan.infeasibleTitle: No crop mix fits these limits
plan.infeasibleSoil: At {{water}} AF per acre, the highest soil score any mix reaches is {{max}}.
plan.infeasibleWaterNeed: To keep a soil minimum of {{soil}}, you need at least {{need}} AF per acre.
plan.infeasibleShare: Your limits on each rotation leave no mix that covers your whole farm.
plan.mathSteps: We tried all 10,626 mixes of the five rotations in 5% steps. We kept only mixes that stay within {{water}} AF per acre in every one of the 20 years and score at least {{soil}} for soil. Among those, we picked the one with the best blend of average profit and worst-years profit for your risk setting ({{risk}} out of 100).

strip.titleBetter: Your suggested plan holds up better in bad years
strip.titleCost: Fitting your water costs {{v}} per acre in your worst years
strip.subtitle: 20 years at a glance: what each plan would have earned in each past year.
strip.how1: Each dot is one past year, from 2005 to 2024. Dots further right earned more per acre.
strip.how2: The shaded area holds the 4 worst years. The red triangle marks their average: that is the worst 1-in-5 years number.
strip.tableCaption: Profit per acre in each past year
strip.aria: Dot chart of 20 past years. Suggested plan worst 1-in-5 years average {{recWorst}} per acre; current plan {{curWorst}} per acre.
strip.axis: Profit per acre in each of the 20 years ($/acre)

trade.title: Playing it safe adds {{gain}} per acre in your worst years and costs {{cost}} in an average year
trade.titleOne: At this water budget, one plan beats every other mix
trade.subtitle: Every dot on the line is a mix that fits {{water}} AF per acre and cannot be beaten on both numbers at once.
trade.how1: Further right is safer: more profit in your worst 1-in-5 years. Higher up is more profit in an average year.
trade.how2: The navy line is the efficient frontier. The cyan star is the plan we suggest for your risk setting. The hollow circle is what you grow today.
trade.how3: Move the water slider. The old line stays for 2 seconds as a dashed line so you can see how much the choices shrink.
trade.keyboard: Efficient frontier chart. Use the arrow keys to step through the plans.
trade.aria: Efficient frontier with {{n}} plans. Suggested plan: {{recAvg}} average, {{recWorst}} in the worst years. Current plan: {{curAvg}} average, {{curWorst}} in the worst years.
trade.legendFrontier: Best plans at this water budget
trade.legendGhost: Before you moved the water slider
trade.caption: Your current plan sits outside the line because it needs more water than your budget. Every plan on the line fits your water. Moving along the line trades average profit for protection in bad years. Less water pulls the whole line down and to the left.
trade.math1: For each of the 10,626 mixes that fit your water and soil limits, we compute two numbers over 2005 to 2024: the average profit and the average of the 4 worst years.
trade.math2: A mix is on the frontier if no other mix beats it on both numbers. Your risk setting picks one point: it maximizes (1 minus risk) times worst-years profit plus risk times average profit.
trade.sliderHelp: Watch the line move. This is the same water budget as on My plan.

compare.finding: {{name}} earns the most for each acre-foot of water: {{v}}
compare.findingSub: When water is the limit, profit per acre-foot matters more than profit per acre. Each card shows when the crop grows, what it earned over 20 years, and what it does for your soil.
compare.math: Each number is a 20-year average for one acre of that rotation alone, using the same sample data as your plan. Per acre-foot divides average profit by average applied water. Worst 1-in-5 is the average of its 4 worst years.

why.lead: Water here is getting scarcer from both ends: less underground, and more needed by every crop in the heat.
why.satVsGround1: Ground gauges measure one well or one field very precisely, but only where someone put a gauge.
why.satVsGround2: Satellites measure every field and every aquifer the same way, every month, so we can compare places and years. We use satellites to see the whole region, and ask you to check the numbers against your own meters.
why.graceTitle: Water stored underground here has dropped about {{v}} cm since 2005
why.graceRes: Monthly, about 300 km grid. Change in water stored on land and underground.
why.graceHow1: The line shows how much more or less water is stored in this area than the 2005 to 2024 average, as a depth of water in centimeters. It rises a little each winter and falls each summer.
why.graceHow2: A falling line means aquifers are being drawn down faster than rain and rivers refill them.
why.graceAria: Line chart of underground water storage from 2005 to 2024, dropping about {{v}} centimeters.
why.heatTitle: Hot days have risen from about {{a}} to {{b}} a year
why.powerRes: Daily weather, about 50 km grid. Days at or above 110°F (43°C).
why.heatHow1: Each bar is one year. Taller bars mean more days at or above 110°F, when crops need the most water and lose the most yield.
why.heatHow2: The plan must fit your water budget even in the hottest of these years.
why.heatCaption: Days at or above 110°F per year
why.heatAria: Bar chart of hot days per year from 2005 to 2024, rising from about {{a}} to {{b}}.
why.et0Title: Crop thirst peaks in {{m}} at about {{v}} mm of water
why.et0Res: Daily weather, about 50 km grid. Reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56).
why.et0How1: Reference ET is how much water a standard grass field would lose in this weather each month.
why.et0How2: Crop water need is reference ET times a crop factor. Summer crops like cotton grow through the peak; winter grains miss it.
why.et0Aria: Line chart of monthly reference evapotranspiration, peaking in {{m}} at about {{v}} millimeters.
why.etTitle: Our water model is within {{v}}% of satellite-measured crop water use
why.etRes: OpenET ensemble with ECOSTRESS, 30 to 70 m, field scale.
why.etHow1: Navy bars are the water each crop uses in our model. Cyan bars are what satellites measured on real fields here.
why.etHow2: Bars of similar height mean the model's water numbers are believable.
why.etCaption: Modeled vs. satellite crop water use (mm per year)
why.etAria: Paired bars for five crops: modeled and satellite water use agree within {{v}} percent.
why.footnote: All four panels use sample series shaped like the real records so the tool can be built and tested. The backend replaces them with the NASA data named under each chart.

stress.profitBetter: In {{year}}, your suggested plan would have earned {{rec}} per acre, more than the {{cur}} your current plan earns on your water
stress.profitWorse: In {{year}}, your suggested plan would have earned {{rec}} per acre vs. {{cur}} for your current plan
stress.profitSub: Profit per acre in that year, after fitting each plan to your water budget.
stress.how1: Each bar is one plan's profit per acre in the year you picked. If a plan needs more water than your budget, the fields it cannot water are left fallow for that year.
stress.how2: Each bar is the water a plan needs per acre in that year. The black line is your budget.
stress.profitAria: Bar chart for {{year}}: suggested plan {{rec}} per acre, current plan {{cur}} per acre.
stress.waterOver: In {{year}}, your current plan needed {{need}} AF per acre, but your budget is {{budget}}
stress.waterFits: In {{year}}, both plans fit your water budget
stress.waterSub: Water needed per acre in that year, compared with your budget.
stress.waterAria: Bar chart for {{year}}: current plan needs {{cur}} AF per acre, suggested plan {{rec}}, budget {{budget}}.
stress.fallowNote: Your current plan did not fit, so its profit above assumes the fields it could not water sat fallow that year.
stress.math1: For each past year we replay both plans with that year's weather and prices. The suggested plan always fits your budget, because the model checks every year.
stress.math2: When the current plan needs more water than the budget, we keep the share of each crop that the water covers and leave the rest fallow at the fallow cost. This is how a water cut usually plays out on a farm.
